title: The Hidden Payment Complexity of Scaling a Platform in Southeast Asia
summary: Scaling a platform across the region? Learn the hidden complexity of payments in Southeast Asia, from local methods and currencies to new platform rules. The post The Hidden Payment Complexity of Scaling a Platform in Southeast Asia appeared first on Xendit .
body_markdown:
On a map, Southeast Asia looks like one market. For a platform that processes payments, it behaves like many. Each country has its own favorite ways to pay, its own currency, its own licensing rules, and, increasingly, its own expectations of what platforms must do for the merchants they serve.


The opportunity is large enough to justify the effort. E-commerce in the region is projected to reach


[$185 billion in GMV in 2025](https://www.bain.com/about/media-center/press-releases/sea/e-conomy-sea-2025/) , and more than 60% of all payments are now digital, according to the e-Conomy SEA 2025 report by Google, Temasek, and Bain & Company.


This guide covers the four areas where payments in Southeast Asia catch scaling platforms off guard: local payment methods, multi-entity setups, currency constraints, and new platform regulation. In this article, the businesses that sell through a platform are called sub-merchants.


Key takeaways


- Each Southeast Asian market has its own set of local payment methods, so a cards-first setup leaves sales on the table.


- Operating in several countries often means running several legal entities, each with its own accounts and verification.


- Currency rules shape how money can move, and splits or transfers across currencies are often restricted.


- New rules in Indonesia and Vietnam give platforms more responsibility for tax collection and sub-merchant verification.


## Fragmented local payment methods


The first surprise is how differently people pay from one country to the next. A platform that launches with cards alone will find that many customers simply prefer something else: a bank transfer in one market, a QR code in another, an e-wallet in a third.


**Market**


**Examples of local payment methods**


Indonesia


Virtual accounts, QRIS, OVO, DANA, GoPay, ShopeePay, Alfamart, Indomaret


Philippines


GCash, Maya, GrabPay, QR Ph, bank direct debit, 7-Eleven and other over-the-counter outlets


Malaysia


FPX online banking, DuitNow, Touch 'n Go, GrabPay, ShopeePay


Thailand


PromptPay, TrueMoney, LINE Pay, mobile banking apps


Vietnam


ZaloPay, Viettel Pay, VNPT Wallet, ShopeePay


Each method also behaves differently after checkout. Some settle the same day, others take longer. Some support refunds through the same channel, others require a separate payout. For a platform, that means every new method adds a new set of rules for when sub-merchants can be paid and how refunds are handled.


## **Multi-entity setups and verification**


The second surprise is structural. To accept local payment methods and settle in local currency, platforms often need a legal entity in each market, or need to onboard sub-merchants that are incorporated locally. A regional platform can end up running a group of entities, each with its own bank accounts, payment accounts, and compliance obligations.


Verification multiplies too. Every entity and every sub-merchant has to complete business verification, and the documents required depend on where the business is incorporated. Xendit, for example, publishes


[separate document requirements](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/verifying-your-account) for Indonesia, the Philippines, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, Hong Kong, and Singapore. A sub-merchant's authorized representative usually has to confirm their identity as part of the process.


For a platform, the practical question is who carries that work. If the platform collects documents itself, it needs a process for every market. If it relies on its payment provider, it needs one that can verify sub-merchants across all the countries it operates in.


***Read also:[Localization vs. Standardization: Building a Payment Strategy for Southeast Asia Expansion](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/localization-vs-standardization-building-a-payment-strategy-for-southeast-asia-expansion/)***


## **Currency constraints**


The third surprise is how much currency shapes the flow of money. A customer in Manila pays in pesos, a customer in Bangkok pays in baht, and each sub-merchant usually wants to be paid in the currency it reports in. Every time those currencies differ, the platform has to decide where conversion happens and who absorbs the cost.


Some of the tools platforms rely on also work only within one currency. On XenPlatform, for example,


[split payments run only within the same currency](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/split-payments) , with support for IDR, PHP, THB, VND, and MYR. A platform that takes commission in Thailand and the Philippines therefore sets up commission rules in each currency, rather than one regional rule.


The practical fix is to design for currencies early. Decide which balances each market holds, when conversion happens, and how commission rules are set up per currency, before the second market goes live, not after the fifth.


***Read also:[Multi-Currency FX and Settlement in Southeast Asia: A Guide for Regional Finance Teams](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/multi-currency-fx-and-settlement-in-southeast-asia-a-guide-for-regional-finance-teams/)***


## **Tightening platform regulation**


The fourth surprise is newer. Regulators across the region are giving platforms more responsibility for the businesses that sell through them. Two recent changes show the direction.


Indonesia: tax collection through marketplaces.


Under Minister of Finance Regulation No. 37 of 2025, appointed e-commerce platforms must


[collect 0.5% income tax on domestic sellers' gross turnover](https://kpmg.com/us/en/taxnewsflash/news/2025/09/tnf-indonesia-income-tax-withholding-obligations-for-e-commerce-platforms-and-online-marketplaces.html) , excluding VAT. In July 2026, the Directorate General of Taxes


[appointed Tokopedia, Shopee, Lazada, and Blibli as the first collection agents](https://news.ddtc.co.id/en/news/1820490/djp-appoints-4-major-marketplaces-as-collection-agents) , with collection starting on August 1, 2026.


Vietnam: seller verification and platform accountability.


Vietnam's Law on E-commerce 2025, Law No. 122/2025/QH15,


[took effect on July 1, 2026](https://kpmg.com/us/en/taxnewsflash/news/2026/06/tnf-vietnam-law-on-e-commerce-2025-effective-july-1-2026.html) . It increases obligations on intermediary platforms for content control and seller verification, and tightens oversight of cross-border e-commerce.


For platforms, the common thread is data. Collecting tax or verifying sellers is only possible if the platform knows exactly who each sub-merchant is and how much it earned. A payment setup that keeps a verified account and a clean transaction history for every sub-merchant makes these obligations far easier to meet.


Regulations change quickly, and the details depend on each platform's situation. Treat this section as context, and confirm your obligations with local legal and tax advisers.


## **How to plan payments for regional growth**


None of these challenges is a reason to stay in one market, but each is easier to solve before launch than after. Before entering a new country, answer five questions:


1. Which local payment methods do customers in this market expect?


Start with the ones your target customers use most.


2. Which entity will collect and settle payments?


Decide whether you need a local entity, or whether you will onboard locally incorporated sub-merchants.


3. How will sub-merchants be verified?


Confirm the documents each market requires and who will collect them.


4. Which currency will each balance hold?


Set up commission rules and payouts per currency from the start.


5. What will regulators expect from you?


Check whether tax collection, seller verification, or reporting obligations apply to platforms in that market.

## **Frequently Asked Questions**


**What makes payments in Southeast Asia different from other regions?**


The region combines several very different markets. Each country has its own popular payment methods, currency, licensing rules, and regulatory expectations, so a setup that works in one market rarely works unchanged in the next.


**Do platforms need a local entity in every Southeast Asian market?**


It depends on the market, the business model, and the payment methods the platform wants to offer. Some platforms set up local entities, while others onboard locally incorporated sub-merchants through a payment provider. Confirm the requirements for each market with local legal advisers.


**Which payment methods should a platform launch with in a new market?**


Start with the methods your target customers already use most, such as QR payments, e-wallets, or bank transfers, then add others as volume grows. Xendit lists the


[payment methods available in each market](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-methods) in its documentation.


**Does Indonesia's 0.5% marketplace tax apply to every platform?**


No. It applies to platforms the Directorate General of Taxes appoints as collection agents. The


[first four appointed in July 2026](https://news.ddtc.co.id/en/news/1820490/djp-appoints-4-major-marketplaces-as-collection-agents) were Tokopedia, Shopee, Lazada, and Blibli, and other platforms that meet the criteria can be appointed later.


**Can a platform split payments across different currencies?**


On XenPlatform,


[splits only happen within the same currency](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/split-payments) . Platforms operating in several markets set up commission rules separately for each supported currency.


**How does Vietnam's new e-commerce law affect platforms?**


The


[Law on E-commerce 2025](https://kpmg.com/us/en/taxnewsflash/news/2026/06/tnf-vietnam-law-on-e-commerce-2025-effective-july-1-2026.html) , effective July 1, 2026, raises intermediary platforms' obligations around seller verification, content control, and data protection, and adds new rules for livestream sales and cross-border e-commerce.
